failing_part: "leaves the exposure's main coefficient and its interval exactly unchanged ... so the repair needs no post-lock check"
narrowest_regime: Holds only if the modifier is coded symmetrically (-1/+1, or centered) or if there is no exposure x modifier term; with 0/1 coding and an interaction it fails.
reason: With Y = b0 + b1 E + b2 M + b3 E*M and M' = 1 - M, the model becomes (b0+b2) + (b1+b3) E - b2 M' - b3 E M': the exposure's main coefficient changes from its effect in one stratum (b1) to its effect in the other (b1+b3), with a different interval, and the intercept also moves. A simulation (n=500) gave the exposure coefficient 0.536 [0.405, 0.667] under one coding and 1.041 [0.896, 1.186] under the swapped coding; only with -1/+1 coding was it unchanged. Frisch-Waugh-Lovell does not imply invariance here, because the recoding changes the column space spanned by E*M relative to E.

citations.cite: Frisch & Waugh 1933, Econometrica 1:387-401; Lovell 1963, JASA 58:993-1010 (FWL theorem; misapplied here)

bite_note: The reported exposure effect becomes the other stratum's conditional effect, so a silent relabel after the lock changes the headline estimate and its CI; a post-lock check is needed.

failing_part: "the smallest gain that matters for every task, including the mean squared error of a numeric outcome in its squared outcome units ... and the Brier score"
narrowest_regime: At most a rough convention for log loss in nats on outcomes that are not rare; it cannot hold for MSE, whose scale is set by the outcome's units.
reason: MSE is in squared outcome units, so a fixed 0.01 depends entirely on the units: for fasting glucose in mg/dL (variance in the hundreds) 0.01 mg^2/dL^2 is a negligible fraction of the variance, while for an outcome measured in thousands of units or as a proportion it is huge or impossible. A unit change (mg/dL to mmol/L) rescales MSE by about 324 and changes the verdict. The Brier score's size depends on prevalence: at 2% prevalence the null Brier is about 0.0196, so a 0.01 gain is half the total and far from 'smallest that matters'. The basis itself says it is 'a convention, not a cited rule', and no methods reason ties 0.01 to any of these scales.
bite_note: It sets the 'better' verdict and the equivalence margin (delta = 0.005) for nested tuning. For a numeric outcome on a large scale, every tiny gain counts as 'better'; on a small scale or with a rare outcome, real gains are dismissed as 'too small to matter whatever the folds say'.

failing_part: "the weight of the largest sample on which any analysis variable was measured — the MEC examination weight ... even when a fasting analyte such as glucose is also analyzed"
narrowest_regime: None as stated. The MEC weight is right only when no variable in the analysis comes from a smaller subsample (no fasting-subsample or dietary-recall variables).
reason: The cited source, the NHANES Tutorials Weighting Module, states the opposite rule: 'You must use the weight of the smallest subpopulation that includes all the variables you want to include in your analysis', meaning 'the weight that is appropriate for the variable of interest that was collected on the smallest number of respondents'. With fasting glucose in the model, the fasting-subsample weight (e.g. WTSAF2YR) applies. The fasting subsample was drawn with its own selection and nonresponse adjustments, so the MEC weight does not represent the population for those rows. 'Keeps the most participants' is not a valid reason: rows without the fasting analyte are dropped from the analysis anyway, and the remaining rows are then wrongly weighted.
bite_note: It changes which weight variable is used, and so the point estimates, standard errors and population inference for every NHANES analysis involving fasting analytes or dietary recalls.

narrowest_regime: Holds generally for squared-error R^2 on a held-out period: point predictions, SSE > 0.
reason: The sum of squares about the opened period's own mean is never larger than the sum about the development mean (the sample mean minimizes the sum of squares), so 1 - SSE/SST_own <= 1 - SSE/SST_dev. The own-mean R^2 is therefore never above the out-of-sample R^2 that uses the development mean (Campbell & Thompson style), which makes it conservative; it is also the default of common tools (sklearn r2_score). The own-mean baseline is an oracle that knows the future period's mean, so the deployable comparison is the model's RMSE against the RMSE of predicting the development mean, as stated.

citations.cite: Campbell & Thompson 2008, Rev Financ Stud 21:1509-1531 (out-of-sample R^2 against the historical mean)

bite_note: The two R^2 versions differ by about (1-R^2)*d^2, where d is the period's mean shift in SD units. For NHANES glucose across cycles d is small, so the reported number barely moves, and the conservative choice cannot overstate performance.

narrowest_regime: A column whose every row has the same value, including no blanks. A column of one value plus blanks (e.g. a checkbox coded 1/blank) is not constant: its missingness pattern is a usable binary variable and must not be caught by this rule.
reason: A truly constant column has zero variance on the analyzed rows. Every learner's fitted function is unchanged by it: it is absorbed by the intercept in GLMs (and makes the design matrix rank-deficient), never splits in trees, and adds a constant to every distance. Excluding it cannot change any estimate or prediction from this table, so no question to the researcher is needed. The caveat is implementation: a distinct-count that drops nulls would wrongly treat '1 or blank' indicator columns as constant.
bite_note: For a truly constant column, excluding it leaves every fitted model and estimate unchanged compared with keeping it or asking. It only avoids a singular design.

failing_part: "a column with exactly two distinct values ... is a category, not an amount" (as a general rule that justifies refusing)
narrowest_regime: True binary attributes coded as two labels (0/1 indicators, yes/no, sex coded 1/2), where the numbers carry no magnitude.
reason: How many distinct values happen to appear does not fix the measurement level. A dose column observed at 10 and 20 mg, a count that happens to take only 0 and 3 in a small sample, or two survey years are still amounts. What is true is that two observed values carry only one contrast, so treating such a column as an amount or as a category differs only in how it is weighted in the distance. Under Gower's coefficient, range-normalized numeric and simple-matching categorical treatment give identical contributions (|x-y|/range is 0 or 1). So the rule is a harmless default for 0/1 codes, but not a fact that warrants refusing the researcher's reading.
bite_note: With two values the only difference is the column's weight: none under Gower, and a rescaling under z-scored k-means. Cluster solutions rarely change materially, though refusing a legitimate 'amount' declaration is a usability cost.

failing_part: "rounds [25, 1,000] ... depth [2, 10] ... learning rate [0.01, 0.3] ... contains the well-performing settings" (the cited source places most best settings outside this box)
narrowest_regime: Small-to-moderate tables where a learning rate of about 0.03-0.3 with at most 1,000 rounds reaches the loss plateau, and as a box that holds near-best (not best) settings, because XGBoost's loss surface is flat.
reason: Probst, Boulesteix & Bischl 2019 (Table 3, AUC) report optimal defaults of nrounds 4168, eta 0.018 and max_depth 13. Across datasets, their q0.05-q0.95 ranges for the best settings are nrounds 920.7-4550.95, eta 0.002-0.355 and max_depth 5.6-14, so the 1,000-round cap excludes roughly 95% of their best configurations, and the depth and learning-rate floors cut off parts of the range. The other ranges are consistent with theirs (child weight 1.3-7.0, lambda 0.008-29.8, subsample 0.55-0.96, colsample_bytree 0.42-0.86). The box therefore relies on eta-rounds trade-offs to reach good performance rather than 'containing' the settings the cited source found. The per-parameter tunabilities they report are small (about 0.001-0.008 AUC), so the practical loss is probably small, but the stated support is misapplied.

citations.cite: Probst, Boulesteix & Bischl 2019, JMLR 20(53):1-32, 'Tunability: importance of hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms', Tables 1 and 3
Chen & Guestrin 2016, KDD, 'XGBoost: a scalable tree boosting system'

bite_note: Because the eta-rounds trade-off and a flat surface make up for the caps, the expected loss compared with Probst's wider space is in the thousandths of AUC. It could matter on large n, where deep trees and more than 1,000 rounds are optimal and early stopping is off.

failing_part: "Each cross-validated score's standard error ... tell whether two models differ"
narrowest_regime: The corrected repeated k-fold t (Nadeau-Bengio variance inflation 1/J + n_test/n_train, df = J-1) as an approximate, often conservative, test of whether two learning algorithms' expected error at training size n(1-1/K) differs. Per-score SEs only when they carry the same correction.
reason: There is no unbiased estimator of the variance of K-fold CV (Bengio & Grandvalet 2004). The naive fold SE of a CV score badly understates uncertainty: in a 10x10-fold simulation (n=200, OLS) it averaged 0.148 against a true across-dataset SD of 0.467, while the corrected SE averaged 0.516. Under a symmetric null, the corrected paired t rejected at 1.8% (nominal 5%) and the naive t at 57%. So the corrected interval is a usable but conservative heuristic, not an exact test. A non-significant result shows the algorithms are not distinguishable at this n, not that the fitted models are equivalent, and CV targets average performance over training sets rather than the performance of the model fitted to these rows (Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani 2024). Replacing a sample-size rule with an interval is sound, but 'tell whether two models differ' overstates what these quantities deliver, and the per-score SE is unspecified.

citations.cite: Nadeau & Bengio 2003, Machine Learning 52:239-281, 'Inference for the generalization error'
Bouckaert & Frank 2004, PAKDD, LNCS 3056:3-12, 'Evaluating the replicability of significance tests for comparing learning algorithms'
Bengio & Grandvalet 2004, JMLR 5:1089-1105, 'No unbiased estimator of the variance of K-fold cross-validation'
Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani 2024, JASA 119:1434-1445, 'Cross-validation: what does it estimate and how well does it do it?'

bite_note: It decides the family-comparison verdicts. If per-score SEs are naive, they produce spurious 'differs' calls. The corrected interval is conservative, so at small n it often returns 'no difference', which researchers may misread as equivalence.

failing_part: "may have changed or been changed by the diet ... so neither model alone is the default" (applied to every follow-up outcome, including randomized diet trials)
narrowest_regime: Observational cohorts where the diet exposure is habitual or predates the baseline measurement, so baseline HbA1c, BP or LDL may be both a confounder (reverse causation, advice-driven diet change) and a mediator of earlier diet.
reason: In cohorts, the baseline level of the outcome's kind has an ambiguous causal role: confounder or mediator. Glymour et al. 2005 (verified) show that baseline adjustment in change analyses can induce bias when the exposure relates to baseline status, and Schisterman, Cole & Platt 2009 (verified) define the overadjustment bias of conditioning on intermediates. A with-and-without pair is therefore a defensible sensitivity default there. In a randomized trial, however, a baseline measured before assignment cannot have been changed by the assigned diet, and baseline-adjusted ANCOVA is the standard, unbiased and more efficient default for a follow-up or change outcome. The statement's regime (any follow-up outcome) does not exclude this case, so 'neither model alone is the default' fails there.

citations.cite: Glymour, Weuve, Berkman, Kawachi & Robins 2005, Am J Epidemiol 162(3):267-278 (PMID 15987729)
Vickers & Altman 2001, BMJ 323:1123 (ANCOVA for baseline in trials)

bite_note: It sets the pre-filled adjustment answer. In trials it replaces the efficient ANCOVA default with a pair, inviting choice between the two models and losing precision. In cohorts it changes which estimates are reported.

failing_part: "values failing these tests are treated as already normalized or log-scale" (and the uncited cut-offs 20 / 100 / 100-fold / 1,000 / 0.5)
narrowest_regime: Canonical raw formats: integer RNA-seq read counts (e.g. HTSeq/featureCounts/STAR gene counts), and raw MS or NMR intensities in the thousands or more. For these the detection direction is right, and genotype dosages 0/1/2 are correctly kept out.
reason: The positive tests flag the textbook raw formats, and the stated rationale checks out: a lognormal with CV 30% has skewness (e^{s2}+2)sqrt(e^{s2}-1) = 0.93, and log2 intensities span far less than 100-fold. The complement fails for common genomics inputs, though. RSEM/Salmon/kallisto estimated counts (e.g. TCGA RSEM 'raw_count') are non-integer, so they fail the whole-number test and are read as normalized despite needing library-size normalization. TPM/FPKM and raw microarray intensities are also non-integer and unlogged yet are 'treated as already normalized or log-scale' under the genomics lens, which has no intensity test. The numeric cut-offs have no cited justification, so their precision is invented even where the direction is right.
bite_note: Missing these cases leaves linear families un-refused and skips the normalization question for estimated-count, TPM/FPKM or raw-array blocks, so researchers fit linear models on heavily skewed, depth-confounded features.

failing_part: "An all-components contrast is undefined on logged components"; also "an average over the analyzed rows at that k" without restricting to rows where the shift is feasible
narrowest_regime: Pairwise donor-to-recipient substitution with log or spline terms, averaged (g-computation) over the rows whose donor intake exceeds k (or after a log1p offset).
reason: By derivation, for Y = ... + b1 f(x1) + b2 g(x2) with total energy fixed, person i's effect of moving k kcal is b1[f(x1i+k)-f(x1i)] + b2[g(x2i-k)-g(x2i)]. That depends on k and the person's intake, so the curve is an average over rows, not b1-b2; this core is correct. The same logic shows an all-components contrast (k kcal into the recipient, taken proportionally or equally from every other component) is perfectly well defined on logged components as a row average. For a proportional cut it is b_j log(1-k/D_i) per donor. What does not exist is a single coefficient contrast, so 'undefined' overstates. Averaging 'over the analyzed rows' also needs a feasibility restriction: for rows with donor intake below k, log(x2-k) is undefined and the shift is off-support (cf. modified treatment policies).

citations.cite: Diaz, Williams, Hoffman & Schenck 2023, JASA 118:846-857 (modified treatment policies; feasibility of shifts)

bite_note: The label of the pairwise curve is right. The only effect is that a researcher told an all-components contrast is 'undefined' may skip a computable estimand, a narrow loss.

failing_part: "at the median without indicators, because their missingness belongs to the upstream process, not the person, and does not exist at the moment of use"
narrowest_regime: Re-imputing flagged values inside each training fold is sound when the upstream method is unrecorded and may have used the outcome or all rows. Dropping indicators is justified only when deployment inputs will be fully measured (never provider-filled) and the original missingness is not informative.
reason: Treating unrecorded upstream fills as missing and re-imputing within folds is good practice: it avoids leakage from an imputation that may have used test rows or the outcome. The stated reasons for median imputation without indicators do not hold in general. The values a provider filled were originally missing for reasons that often reflect the person (tests not ordered, nonresponse), so the missingness can be informative. If deployment data pass through the same provider pipeline, the fill flag does exist at the moment of use. The cited Sisk et al. 2023 (verified) studied multiple and regression imputation, not median imputation, and found that 'missing indicators improved model performance in many cases', harming only under outcome-dependent missingness. TRIPOD+AI item 11 is a reporting item, not a method recommendation.

citations.cite: Sisk, Sperrin, Peek, van Smeden & Martin 2023, Stat Methods Med Res 32(8):1461-1477 (PMID 37105540)
Collins et al. 2024, BMJ 385:e078378, TRIPOD+AI statement, item 11

bite_note: When the original missingness is informative and persists at deployment, dropping indicators and using median fills can lower discrimination and distort calibration and linear-model coefficients, compared with regression imputation plus indicators.
